posts.content_md:
Colin,

Thanks for the link to Adam’s truly “great laser”. I try not to meddle in these matters any more than absolutely necessary, but here I may have some advice to offer that might actually be construed as constructive. Whenever I’m about to tape together a laser I ask myself “do I really need to go out and buy a new roll of electrical tape – couldn’t I just make do with the duct tape that I bought to reattach the bumper on my Pinto?” The answer is of course not! By saving $2, I’ve actually reduced the cost of Adams laser by almost 1% and who’s gonna know? OK new tape sticks a little better but that can be a negative (as I’ve learned the hard way) because when the laser acts up and you have to go in and shim up a mirror mount or glue-up a pesky water leak … hey, no problem.

posts.author: ron olson
posts.post_subject: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.content_md:
Guys,

I hate to be the bearer of bad news but this is supposed to be a forum about pulsed holography and pulsed holography requires a very good (typically very expensive) laser. While I can't really comment on the (questionable) temporal coherence, the spatial profile from Adam's laser is totally unsuitable for holography and no amount of minor tinkering will change that. Building a short cavity TEMoo resonator with anything in the way of spatial and temporal coherence is extremely difficult - believe me I know from experience. Forum contributors really have to start treating this technique more like serious photography than like an 8th grade science project. Getting “attaboys” from fellow tinkerers does absolutely nothing to improve the technique and as I continue to preach: holography is being judged by a viewing public that cares not one iota about “how you did it” or worse yet, “how you made do” - only about “what you did”.

posts.topic_title: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.author: ron olson
posts.post_subject: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.content_md:
Adam,

50mJ of green light in a single spatial mode is a lot of energy for a short cavity single mode laser. To maintain a truly TEMoo beam will require an intra-cavity aperture (pinhole) <1mm for a 25cm cavity. Without an extremely sophisticated resonator design (a la Gaussian mirrors) you'll be lucky to get 2mJ of high-quality Q-switched green light. Portraits aside, I struggle lighting still lifes with less than 250mJ. Check around (eBay, Laser Resale, et al) for obsoleted Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers. I bought my original hardware kit used (gov't surplus) and reconfigured it to produce 1J at 532nm for ~$5k. I have mentioned this before but it's worth repeating that if you remove (entirely) the cost of my laser, I still am looking at more than $100k in studio hardware every time I walk through the door and, in addition I spend >$10k a year on film. These little (SSY?) mini-YAGs are not the way to go except as proof of principle and I would hope we're a little past that. If you like fast cars or fast boats - you're going to pay a price. If you like fast exposures what makes you think it will be any different?

> These little (SSY?) mini-YAGs are not the way to go except as proof of principle and I would hope we're a little past that.

I have to disagree with you Ron. A few years ago anyone could have told us that making good holograms with a laser diode was impossible. Now, many people are doing it. Then people told that it was impossible to make long term exposures with laser diodes due to mode-hops. I have been regularly doing 45 minute exposures on MBDCG without a single mode hop. And that with a diode laser that cost me less than 100 Dollar to build, compared to a professional Spectra Physics 125 that costs more than 5K. 

I think that all experiments, especially those of people who are on a limited budget are admirable and will advance the science in many directions, and are worth much praise. In that respect, the experiments with pulsed "mini-YAG's" are just as important. Belittleling the effort of a young and enthousiastic experimenter does no good for anyone. Keep in mind that some of us like to do the pretty holograms, some of us like to experiment with emulsions, and some of us like to experiment with laser technology. All are important to this forum and have something to contribute.

I will say: WELL DONE ADAM!!! I look forward to see how your MOPA experiments will turn out.

posts.topic_title: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.author: ron olson
posts.post_subject: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.content_md:
Again it would seem that I’m the bad guy belittling the efforts of a young, energetic enthusiast. If Adam equipped with his mini-YAG can produce an image portfolio that enhances holographics – then more power to him. However I have serious problems with encouraging efforts that I sincerely believe lack even a remote chance of artistic success.

Hans, comparing the holographic suitability of an early DPSS laser to that of a mini-YAG is nonsense. In the case of the former: no one but a fool couldn’t foresee that DPSS lasers would evolve in parallel with the IR laser diodes pumping them. To anyone with a laser engineering background this was inevitable - the only question was “when?” as determined by price point. But as to the latter: flashlamp pumped mini-YAG lasers aren’t evolving – they’re on the down side of the curve rapidly being made obsolete by diode pumped and/or solid-state alternatives. You can’t just wish a laser head to have more pump energy or better coupling efficiency nor can you conjure up coherence length or beam uniformity. Perhaps you know of a high-resolution photo emulsion with ~100 times the sensitivity of silver halide or perhaps you think there’s a market for (or on a less commercial note: "significant personal pride in creating") postage-stamp sized images of postage stamps? For $1500 you can get a nice 100mW CW Coherent laser with oodles of coherence and a very nice beam. This is the way to approach holography on a budget – not with a potentially dangerous hardware package that is totally ill-suited for graphic imaging.

posts.topic_title: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.author: ron olson
posts.post_subject: Adam's Pulsed Laser on the Wiki!
posts.content_md:
Adam, 

If I understand correctly that your intent is indeed to produce ~1cm square transmission H1’s – your mini-YAG will probably suffice. As to the use of a passive Q-switch as an etalon: typically Q-switches a) aren’t cut to be extremely plane-parallel and b) aren’t positioned on high-precision adjustable mounts. If you’re using a dye cuvette, I believe they can be specified with parallel surfaces – but the price of the cuvette will be more than your laser. Passive Q-switches (dyes or crystals) tend to discriminate in favor of strong modes, suppressing weaker ones so you may get the occasional robust pulse exhibiting longer coherence. The rod itself may be acting as an etalon as may the output coupler especially if it’s uncoated. For a passive Q-switch to work properly, you should attempt to stay at or very near lasing threshold. Brewsters windows aligned correctly influence primarily the beams polarization and (to a lesser degree) cavity losses.
